name: Urban Vegetation Types – Perceived Ecosystem Services (Singapore)
description:
Faithful replication of Drillet, Fung, Leong, Sachidhanandam, Edwards & Richards (2020), "Urban Vegetation Types are Not Perceived Equally in Providing Ecosystem Services and Disservices", Sustainability 12:2076. Using the paper's published questionnaire, Singapore residents (1) say which of five vegetation types they have in their neighbourhood, (2) rate agreement with 15 benefit statements (e.g. "It provides me with shade") and 10 nuisance statements (e.g. "It poses a risk of spreading mosquito-borne diseases") about vegetation, (3) pick, for each statement, the type it applies to best (grass, tree, shrub, tree planted over shrub, secondary forest, or N/A), shown with the paper's five photographs, and (4) rank the types they would like to see planted near home. In the original online survey (n = 1,000), benefits outweighed nuisances; over 80% valued shade and air quality; trees were most linked to cooling and clean air, and secondary forest to learning about nature and wildlife.

Photographs and wording: Drillet et al. (2020), Figure 1 and supplementary questionnaire, CC BY 4.0. Used with credit for research; the template is removed if the authors object.

Differences from the original study: (1) only the vegetation part of the published questionnaire is included; the sections on outdoor activities, birds and the Nature Relatedness scale are left out (they are cut off in the supplement or belong to a separate study); (2) the residential postal code question is left out for privacy; (3) age is typed in instead of chosen from a list; (4) ranking is done by tapping the photos in order instead of choosing rank numbers from drop-downs; (5) the consent statements are shortened.
author: Drillet, Fung, Leong, Sachidhanandam, Edwards & Richards
